paper_b.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Integers

metadata.description: Both papers achieve fully homomorphic encryption via the same blueprint: somewhat-homomorphic encryption restricted to permitted (low-depth/low-degree) circuits, plus Gentry-style bootstrapping after squashing the decryption circuit (with a sparse subset-sum hint). They differ fundamentally in algebraic substrate: Gentry instantiates the abstract ring/ideal scheme over polynomial rings R = Z[x]/(f(x)) and ideal lattices, with security reducing to BDDP/SIVP on ideal lattices (plus SSSP for squashing); DGHV instantiates the same blueprint over the integers (R = Z, I = (2)) with security reducing to the approximate-gcd problem (plus SSSP). Both papers are PDF-fallback extractions, so notation differs but the structural correspondence is tight.

matches.explanation: Both define correctness of homomorphic decryption: Decrypt(sk, Evaluate(pk, C, ciphertexts)) equals C(plaintexts). Statements differ only in the (negligible-probability) qualifier.

Compactness: a polynomial-size bound on the decryption circuit / on Evaluate output, independent of |C|. Same standard FHE definition, slight phrasing difference (polynomial bound on D_E size vs polynomial bound on Evaluate output size).

Fully homomorphic encryption: compactly evaluates all boolean circuits (Gentry splits into 'compactly evaluates' and 'fully homomorphic'; DGHV combines them into a single definition). Also covers DGHV's notion of homomorphic for a class C.

Leveled FHE definition: a family {E^(d) : d in Z+} sharing one decryption circuit, evaluating depth-d circuits with poly(lambda, d, |C|) complexity. Paper-A-original concept; paper B obtains depth-d FHE via Gentry's bootstrapping (cited as TP304.1) but does not extract the leveled-FHE definition as a separate node.

Augmented decryption circuit: copies of D_E joined by a single gate g (over add and mult mod 2 in DGHV). DGHV cites this directly from Gentry [7]; the definitions are the same up to the choice of gate set.
Bootstrappable encryption: D_E(Gamma) is contained in C_E (the homomorphic-correctness class). DGHV cites this from Gentry; identical definition.

Gentry's bootstrapping theorem: a bootstrappable scheme yields a depth-d homomorphic scheme for any d (leveled FHE). DGHV cites this verbatim as Theorem 2.7 (Gentry); paper A is the original. Origin in DGHV is external pointing to Gentry.

Permitted circuits: paper A defines them abstractly (g(C) maps X_Enc^t into X_Dec, i.e., generalized circuit output stays within the decryptable region); paper B defines them concretely (mod-2 arithmetic circuits whose generalized integer-circuit output stays within magnitude bound 2^{alpha(eta-4)}, equivalent to noise staying below p/2). Same conceptual role: the class for which the somewhat-homomorphic scheme is correct.

Depth/degree bound for permitted circuits. Paper A's Theorem 1.4.1 / 7.3.2 bounds depth by log log r_Dec - log log (gamma_Mult * r_Enc); paper B's Eq.(1) and Lemma 3.5 bound polynomial degree by (eta - 4 - log|f|)/(rho'+2). Both express the noise-growth ceiling that determines homomorphic capacity, in the respective metrics (norm under polynomial multiplication vs absolute value under integer multiplication).

Correctness of the somewhat-homomorphic scheme on its permitted-circuit class. Paper A's Theorem 5.2.6 is the abstract version; paper B's Lemma 3.3 is the concrete integer version. Both have proofs decomposing fresh ciphertexts plus an inductive bound on evaluated ciphertexts.

Proofs of somewhat-homomorphic correctness. Paper A decomposes psi_k = pi_k + i_k + j_k and reduces mod B^sk_J then mod B_I. Paper B uses Lemma A.1 (fresh ciphertext c = ap + (2b+m), |2b+m| <= tau*2^{rho+3}) and Lemma A.2 (evaluated ciphertext has |2b+m| < p/8). Both are the same structural argument: bound the noise of fresh ciphertexts, propagate through the circuit, show the result is decoded correctly.

Proof of paper A's depth-vs-error theorem (Theorem 7.3.2): induction on circuit depth showing r_d <= (gamma_Mult * r_E)^{2^d}. Paper B's analogous bound (Eq.(1) and Lemma 3.5) is stated without an extracted proof node; the noise analysis is folded into the somewhat-homomorphic correctness proof PP304.1.

Somewhat-homomorphic scheme. Paper A gives an abstract ring/ideal scheme (AP303.1) instantiated over Z[x]/(f) and ideal lattices (AP303.4); paper B gives the concrete integer scheme (AP304.1) where R = Z, I = (2), and J is the principal ideal generated by p. Same KeyGen/Encrypt/Evaluate/Decrypt skeleton, totally different algebraic substrate (this is the central CF axis of the pair).

Composite L2 alignment of the two somewhat-homomorphic schemes' algorithm steps. Paper A's KeyGen samples ideal-lattice bases via RandomizeIdeal/WeakRandomIdealGen; paper B's KeyGen samples an odd eta-bit integer p plus tau+1 noisy multiples. Encrypt/Evaluate/Decrypt steps mirror each other (sample noise, mod public-key reduction, evaluate in the ring, mod-then-mod decryption), but the steps are not in 1:1 correspondence. Emitted as parent-first composite per L2 rule.

Squashing transformation: enlarge the public key with vectors {t_i}/{y_i} that contain a sparse subset summing to (a multiple of) the inverse secret key, replacing decryption's costly division/rounding by a sparse subset sum. The structure (SplitKey + ExpandCT + reduced Decrypt; or augmented KeyGen + augmented Encrypt + reduced Decrypt) is identical; sparse subset has size theta = lambda in B and gamma_subsetsize(n) in A.

Composite L2 alignment of the squashed-scheme steps. Both produce the hint vector(s) (t_i in J^{-1} / y_i = u_i/2^kappa rationals), expand the ciphertext via multiplication c_i = t_i * psi or z_i = c* y_i mod 2, then decrypt by selecting the sparse subset, summing, rounding, and subtracting modulo I or modulo 2. Step granularity differs but each side covers the same operations.

Bootstrappability of the squashed scheme (statements + proofs). Paper A's Thm 1.5.2 / Thm 10.3.1 give the depth-of-decryption bound (~ (log|T|)^{1+o(1)}) under which D_E is in C_E; paper B's Lemma 6.1 + Theorem 6.2 establish the analogous result with degree <= 64*lambda*log^2(lambda), with proofs PP304.3 (squashed correctness via |sum s_i Delta_i| <= 1/16 and |c* Delta_p| < 1/16) and PP304.4 (bootstrappability via 3-step decomposition). Same conclusion via the same Hamming-weight / three-for-two reduction; paper A states only the correctness statement nodes without separated proofs.

Hamming-weight bit-polynomial / rounded-sum-via-symmetric-polynomials lemma. Paper A's Lemma 9.0.3 (rounded sum via symmetric polynomials) and the constant-depth XOR-style summation match paper B's Lemma 6.3 (which paper B credits to Boyar-Peralta-Pochuev). Both express W_i (the i-th bit of Hamming weight) as the elementary symmetric polynomial e_{2^i} mod 2 of degree exactly 2^i, and sum O(theta) rationals via this trick.

Composite L2: the three-step decryption-as-polynomial decomposition is shared. Paper A's squashed-Decrypt steps (multiply via M, sum sparse subsets, round via symmetric polynomials, subtract) correspond to paper B's three proof steps inside PP304.4 (multiply s_i z_i, reduce Theta rationals to n+1 via Hamming-weight columns, sum n+1 rationals via three-for-two). Same algorithmic decomposition; one paper places it in the algorithm description, the other in the bootstrappability proof.

Sparse Subset Sum Problem (SSSP). Paper A formalises both decision and search SSSP (a_i in [-q/2, q/2] with hidden sparse subset summing to 0 mod q); paper B references the same SSSP / low-weight knapsack assumption to justify the squashed-scheme hint. The hardness assumption underpinning squashing is the same in both papers; paper A introduced it for the ideal-lattice setting and paper B reuses it.

Sparse Vector Subset Sum Problem (SVSSP) is paper A's intermediate step in reducing concrete SplitKey to SSSP through the ideal-lattice machinery; paper B has no analogue because it works directly over the integers and does not factor through ideals.

Security reduction of the somewhat-homomorphic scheme to the underlying hard problem. Paper A: SplitKey -> SVSSP -> SSSP -> Search SSSP via Goldreich-Levin (a chain of three theorems plus the squashing security hybrid). Paper B: a single reduction of semantic security to the (rho, eta, gamma)-approximate-gcd problem via the four-step Learn-LSB / binary-GCD construction. Different target hardness assumptions (lattice/SSSP vs approximate-gcd), but the architecture (advantage transfer plus bit-by-bit recovery via an LSB oracle / Goldreich-Levin) is parallel.

Composite L2: proof-step decompositions of the security-to-hardness reductions. Paper A uses a 4-step hybrid argument (Game 0/1 + B_0 + B_1 + combine); paper B uses a 5-step explicit construction (build pk + Learn-LSB + binary-GCD + recover p + analyse success). The high-level move (use the adversary's bit-prediction advantage to extract a hidden integer) is the same; the mechanics differ because the hard problem differs.

Leftover Hash Lemma (HILL): both cite the same lemma with the (1/2) sqrt(|Y|/|X|)-uniform bound. Both have origin: external citing the same source (Hastad-Impagliazzo-Levin-Luby / Impagliazzo-Levin-Luby variants).

Subset-sum LHL and reduction-ciphertext-distribution lemma are paper-B-specific instantiations of the LHL for showing that the public-key encryption distribution under the reduction matches the real Encrypt distribution (using x_{T+1} = sum s_i x_i mod M). Paper A uses the abstract LHL without an explicit subset-sum instantiation.

Paper B's preliminary definitions of 2-universal hash family and epsilon-uniform distribution are external (textbook) and used only inside Lemma 3.1; paper A uses LHL but does not state these definitions explicitly (they are folded into LP303.1's citation).

Underlying hard problem. Paper A's hardness chain rests on lattice problems: SVP, CVP, SIVP, BDDP, HBDDP, decision BDDP for ideal lattices, WBDDP. Paper B's security rests entirely on the (rho, eta, gamma)-approximate-gcd problem (find an odd eta-bit p given polynomially many integers q_i*p + r_i with |r_i| < 2^rho). Both are paper-original parametric problem definitions; they play the same role (the assumed-hard problem the scheme reduces to) but are mathematically very different (lattice geometry vs integer GCD).

Paper B's explicit parameter-constraint assumption (rho = omega(log lambda), eta >= rho * Theta(lambda log^2 lambda), gamma = omega(eta^2 log lambda), tau >= gamma + omega(log lambda)) is paper-B-original. Paper A states analogous parameter conditions inline within theorem hypotheses rather than as a single assumption node.

Paper B's squashing parameters (kappa = gamma*eta/rho', theta = lambda, Theta = omega(kappa log lambda)) are paper-B-specific instantiations. Paper A states the analogous conditions abstractly via gamma_setsize(n), gamma_subsetsize(n) (already covered by AP303.5 squashing match).

Paper A explicitly defines semantic security (CPA/CCA1/CCA2). Paper B uses the standard semantic-security notion implicitly without a node-level definition; this is a paper-A-original presentation choice with no atomic counterpart in B.

Statistical circuit privacy is a paper-A-original notion (used for the random-oracle FHE construction TP303.11 and for compressed ciphertexts). Paper B's compression algorithm AP304.3 also uses circuit privacy informally but the explicit definition is not extracted.

Paper A's Ideal Membership Problem and the abstract semantic-security-via-IMP theorem are an intermediate abstraction that paper B does not have (paper B reduces directly to approximate-gcd without going through an IMP-style problem).
Ideal Coset Problem and the corresponding semantic-security reduction (Theorem 5.3.1) are paper-A-original and lattice-specific; no integer counterpart in paper B.

Auxiliary abstract-scheme definitions: generalized circuit g(C), X_Enc/X_Dec, valid ciphertexts, r_Enc/r_Dec radii. Paper B implicitly uses analogous notions (the integer scheme has its own implicit X_Enc, X_Dec, noise radii) but does not factor them out as named definitions.

SplitKey distinguishing problem (abstract and concrete versions) is paper-A-original; the squashing security of paper B is reduced directly to the underlying integer scheme's semantic security plus SSSP-style hardness without an intermediate SplitKey problem.
Inner IMP (IIMP) / Modified IIMP (MIIMP) chain and the security-to-IIMP-to-MIIMP-to-HBDDP-to-IVIP reductions are paper-A-original and entirely lattice-specific; paper B has no analogous chain.

Ideal SIVP / Inverse Ideal SIVP machinery and IVIP reductions are paper-A-original. They are the worst-case-to-average-case lattice reductions that ground paper A's security; paper B's worst-case ground is the assumed average-case hardness of approximate-gcd, which is treated atomically rather than reduced to a worst-case lattice problem.

Ring-theoretic and ideal-lattice technical lemmas (circulant ring expansion, transference lemmas, dual-inverse length, rotation-basis tweaks, probability-mass ratio for sub-lattices). Paper-A-original lattice machinery; no integer-scheme counterpart in paper B.

Geometric characterisation of r_Dec via inscribed ball radius is paper-A-original; paper B's analogue (the noise tolerance |2b+m| < p/8) is a scalar bound rather than a ball-inscribed-in-parallelepiped argument.

Lemmas about RandomizeIdeal output distribution and inverse-of-near-e_1 vectors. Paper-A-original ideal-randomization machinery; paper B does not need worst-case-to-average-case randomisation because approximate-gcd is assumed average-case hard directly.
Worst-case/average-case BDDP reductions, RandomizeIdeal' properties, RandomIdealGen sampling theorems, and the WBDDP-to-HBDDP reduction. Paper-A-original; no counterpart in paper B.

Paper-A semantic-security theorems for the squashed scheme (TP303.3), the leveled scheme (TP303.9), the KDM-secure-bootstrap variant (TP303.10), and the random-oracle variant (TP303.11). Paper B does not present analogous variant-FHE security theorems.

Correctness and Evaluate-complexity of the leveled FHE construction (Theorems 4.2.1, 4.2.2). These accompany TP303.1 and play out the bootstrapping construction concretely; paper B states only the bootstrapping consequence (TP304.3) without separating leveled-correctness and Evaluate-complexity nodes.
Polynomial-ring expansion factor theorems (gamma_Mult(R) bounds) are paper-A-original lattice machinery; the integer scheme has no analogous expansion factor.

Recrypt (bootstrapping refresh) is the central paper-A algorithm that homomorphically evaluates D_E on encrypted secret-key bits. Paper B inherits Recrypt via Theorem 2.7 (their TP304.1) but does not present it as a separate algorithm node; the bootstrapping is treated as a black-box transformation given by Gentry.

Paper A's generic leveled FHE algorithm (the d+1 key chain plus Augment+Reduce) is the explicit construction behind Gentry's bootstrapping theorem. Paper B does not extract this construction as a node, again because it cites the result as a black box.

RandomizeIdeal, RandomizeIdeal' (classical variant), WeakRandomIdealGen, the concrete IdealGen, and Kalai's algorithm. Paper-A-original (or cited) ideal-sampling machinery for worst-case-to-average-case reductions; entirely absent from paper B's integer-arithmetic setting.

Paper B's distribution D_{gamma,rho}(p) (samples x = pq + r near a multiple of p) is the concrete noisy-multiples-of-p distribution underlying the integer scheme; paper A's analogous notion (sampler Samp(B_I, x) producing x + r*s for short r) is wrapped inside the abstract scheme rather than extracted as a separate distribution definition.

DGHV's ciphertext-compression scheme (Appendix D) compresses ciphertexts to RSA-modulus size via a cyclic group of order divisible by p, with security reduced to the decision subgroup problem of Gentry-Ramzan. Paper A does not have a ciphertext-compression layer; this is a paper-B-specific contribution leveraging integer arithmetic and RSA-style groups.

DGHV's remarks: 'permitted but not shallow' (the Hamming-weight subroutine's circuit is non-shallow yet permitted because the polynomials it computes are low-degree, justified by Lemma 3.5); Howgrave-Graham's two-element approximate-gcd lattice attack; and the SDA / Lagarias LLL-based attack. Paper-B-specific motivation/parameter remarks; paper A's analogous discussions are absorbed into formal theorems rather than remarks.

Paper-A remarks (Recrypt implies proxy re-encryption; WeakEncrypt relaxation) are auxiliary observations with no paper-B counterpart. (Aux nodes; included here because they are paper-origin remarks with substantive content.)

Paper-A discussion of restricting plaintext space to {0,1} during bootstrapping and the corresponding open problem (avoiding this restriction). Paper B fixes plaintexts in {0,1} as the only choice via its mod-2 design; the question does not arise in the same form.

DGHV's open problem on improving FHE efficiency (currently O(lambda^10) for the somewhat-homomorphic part) is paper-B-original. Paper A's open problems concern the {0,1}-plaintext restriction, not bit-complexity per ciphertext.
